title: Couples Discount

jokes.text: Jim explains he got on his hands and knees begging partners to switch a Tuesday for a Thursday, then says 'Alakazam' — and then immediately reveals they need an extra day next week.
jokes.setup: Jim romanticizes being in the same city as Pam for Valentine's Day as 'magic'
jokes.punchline: 'Alakazam' deflates the romance immediately, then the favor owed next week undercuts it further — the magic trick cost him more than it gained
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim move — undercut romance with logistical reality. The 'Alakazam' word choice is sharp and specific. The double-undercut (he did the magic trick but now owes a day) is well-structured. Not exceptional but solid opener.

jokes.text: 'And poof, he disappears.' Erin's talking-head confessional where she immediately pivots from Jim and Pam's romantic moment to announcing she's breaking up with Andy.
jokes.setup: Erin observes Jim magically disappearing like a magician, then seems to be reflecting warmly on the couple
jokes.punchline: She abruptly announces Andy is a 'big jerk' and she's dumping him — 'Bam, Andy! How do ya like me now?' — completely shattering the Valentine's Day warmth
jokes.explanation: 'Bam, Andy! How do ya like me now?' is perfectly Erin — childlike aggression delivered with complete sincerity. The tonal whiplash from romantic observation to breakup declaration is well-executed and character-specific.

jokes.text: Jim's talking-head comparing Erin wanting to do 'whatever he'd like' before the Andy breakup to his childhood dog who got sent to a farm — 'on his last day, we did everything he loved.'
jokes.setup: Jim notes Erin says she'll do whatever he wants today
jokes.punchline: He compares the situation to his dying dog's last day — Jim is the dying dog being given a 'fun day' before the bad news
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely excellent. The 'sent to a farm' euphemism layered on top of Jim realizing he's the dying dog is dark and structurally elegant. It works on two levels: the euphemism itself is funny, and the self-aware application to his own situation is sharp. Jim's deadpan delivery implied here makes it land. Strong candidate for episode's best.

jokes.text: Jim immediately asking 'Wanna play catch in the parking lot?' after the dying-dog speech, and Erin cheerfully agreeing.
jokes.setup: Jim has just compared himself to a dying dog whose last day was spent doing fun things
jokes.punchline: He immediately enacts the metaphor by doing the most dog-like activity — playing catch — and neither character acknowledges the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the dying-dog bit. The joke is in the commitment to the metaphor without explaining it. Maximum economy — two words ('play catch') do all the work. Rewatch bonus because you see it differently knowing the setup.

jokes.text: Dwight talking to a pretend 'Andy' — his imagination — and doing a nonsense voice ('Rink-a-dit doo, rika-doot-deet doo') to represent Andy's response, then saying 'I really like Andy these days. He's pretend, and he does exactly as I tell him to.'
jokes.setup: Real Andy is away; Dwight has been managing himself
jokes.punchline: Dwight has invented an imaginary Andy who compliments him and signs off on everything — complete with a made-up voice — and he's genuinely content with this arrangement
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Dwight. The 'Rink-a-dit doo' nonsense voice for imaginary Andy, combined with Dwight's sincere satisfaction, is exceptional character comedy. Only Dwight would invent an imaginary manager and prefer him. The fear of 'pretend Dwight' in the follow-up line adds perfect absurdist escalation.

jokes.text: 'Andy left a carton of milk in the fridge, so I've been sneaking a little bit every day for the last three months. It's been yummy. But now Andy's coming back. So, I guess it's good-bye, chunky lemon milk.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has been drinking Andy's abandoned milk for three months
jokes.punchline: He bids farewell to what is clearly badly spoiled milk — 'chunky lemon milk' — with genuine wistfulness, as if losing a friend
jokes.explanation: 'Chunky lemon milk' is a truly inspired phrase — it perfectly captures three-month-old spoiled milk and the horror that Kevin not only drank it but enjoyed it. The wistful farewell tone transforms this from gross-out humor into character comedy. This is among the episode's best jokes. Kevin's specific obliviousness to food standards is perfectly distilled here.

jokes.text: 'I wish Andy had stayed on his trip. I say we all have one last fun, boss-less day.'
jokes.setup: Andy is returning and the office has enjoyed his absence
jokes.punchline: Oscar, typically the voice of reason, openly admits he wishes the boss had never come back
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the mini-mall plot but not particularly clever. The joke is just 'we liked having no boss' — nothing specific or surprising.

jokes.text: Meredith suggests they 'get some booze and some cocaine and just blow it out, no consequences' for their last boss-less day.
jokes.setup: Oscar suggests a fun, consequence-free last day
jokes.punchline: Meredith's version of 'fun' is cocaine and booze — delivered as if it were a perfectly reasonable suggestion
jokes.explanation: Reliable Meredith character comedy. The deadpan delivery of 'booze and cocaine' as a sincere suggestion is well-integrated with her character. Not a fresh joke type but executed efficiently.

jokes.text: Phyllis describes the couples discount at the mini-mall, then adds: 'if you don't have one of those, you can probably just bring whoever it is you use to kill your loneliness.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis describes the 20% couples discount for husbands or boyfriends
jokes.punchline: Her matter-of-fact description of bringing 'whoever you use to kill your loneliness' is unexpectedly bleak and specific
jokes.explanation: 'Whoever you use to kill your loneliness' is a genuinely dark and poetic phrase delivered in Phyllis's characteristically gentle tone. The contrast between her warm delivery and the bleak sentiment works well.

jokes.text: Stanley offers to pretend to be Phyllis's husband, then adds: 'I'm already sick of you, so it'll seem realistic.'
jokes.setup: Stanley volunteers to be Phyllis's fake husband for the discount
jokes.punchline: His justification — that his contempt for her makes the marriage seem authentic — is both an insult and a logical argument simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Excellent. The joke is perfectly economical and deeply character-specific. Stanley's contempt for everyone around him, and his deadpan logic that mutual annoyance = realistic marriage, is sharp writing. The line doubles as an insult and a practical argument, which is the mark of well-layered comedy.

jokes.text: Phyllis mentions the nail salon uses 'a watch repair kit' on her feet.
jokes.setup: Phyllis promotes the nail salon at the mini-mall
jokes.punchline: The detail that they use a watch repair kit — tools for tiny, precise work — implies her feet are so bad they require specialized delicate instruments
jokes.explanation: Specific and unexpected. 'Watch repair kit' is a funny detail that implies extreme delicacy or extreme grossness (or both) without over-explaining. Good economy.

jokes.text: Oscar says 'I'll be your foot buddy' to Phyllis with genuine excitement about the nail salon.
jokes.setup: Phyllis describes getting her feet detailed at the nail salon
jokes.punchline: Oscar enthusiastically volunteers to be her 'foot buddy' — his excitement is disproportionate and slightly absurd
jokes.explanation: Mild character beat. Gets a small laugh from Oscar's earnestness but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Clark agrees to be Angela's fake boyfriend for the couples discount: 'That's what I do.' — delivered as a weary statement of his role in the office.
jokes.setup: Angela asks Clark to be her fake boyfriend for the discount
jokes.punchline: 'That's what I do' — Clark's resigned acceptance of being used as a prop implies this is a pattern, which is both sad and funny
jokes.explanation: Four words doing a lot of work. The implied history of Clark being used as a prop is conveyed entirely through tone. Good economy, decent character specificity.

jokes.text: Kevin awkwardly asks Darryl to pretend to be a couple for the discount. Darryl flatly says 'No.' Then immediately says 'Yes. Yes. Why wouldn't I?'
jokes.setup: Kevin nervously asks Darryl to fake-couple up for the discount
jokes.punchline: Darryl's instant 'No' followed by an equally instant reversal ('Yes. Yes. Why wouldn't I?') — the reversal is funnier for being so immediate and delivered as if the 'No' never happened
jokes.explanation: The structure here is tight: the 'No' is the setup, the immediate 'Yes. Yes. Why wouldn't I?' is a double punchline. Darryl's need to perform nonchalance about pretending to be gay while being slightly (hilariously) flustered is well-captured in minimal words.

jokes.text: Kevin tries to coach Darryl on pretending to be gay; Darryl snaps 'Stop talking about it. I said I'm fine with it.' Then they both look at the chocolates and simultaneously agree they're terrible.
jokes.setup: Darryl insists he's totally comfortable pretending to be gay
jokes.punchline: His emphatic over-protesting ('Stop talking about it') is the joke — classic protesting too much — immediately defused by both men agreeing the chocolates are gross
jokes.explanation: The protest-too-much joke is familiar but efficiently executed. The pivot to agreeing about the chocolates is a nice beat that defuses the tension naturally.

jokes.text: Jim's talking-head: Brian made a lunch reservation at State Street Grill. Pam: 'Oh my God, that's so romantic.' Jim: 'It's with Brian and Alyssa.' Pam: 'Oh my God, that's less romantic.'
jokes.setup: Jim mentions they have a Valentine's Day lunch reservation at a romantic restaurant
jokes.punchline: It's with another couple — Pam's deflation ('that's less romantic') is perfectly calibrated
jokes.explanation: Tight two-beat structure. Pam's mirrored response ('that's less romantic') is economical and funny. The parallel phrasing is the craft — it's a small piece of writing wit.

jokes.text: Nail salon worker recognizes Phyllis ('Oh, tiny foot lady is back') and gets excited, calling for the baby clipper.
jokes.setup: The group arrives at the nail salon
jokes.punchline: The worker's enthusiasm for Phyllis's tiny feet — 'Get the baby clipper!' — implies her feet are comically, abnormally small, subverting expectations since Phyllis is a large woman
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the watch repair kit setup. 'Tiny foot lady' and 'baby clipper' are both strong specific details. The visual comedy of Phyllis's incongruously small feet pays off an earlier hint.

jokes.text: The nail salon worker tells Clark to take off his glasses. After he does, she declares: 'Your boyfriend. He look like a pretty girl.'
jokes.setup: Clark and Angela are posing as a couple; the worker asks Clark to remove his glasses
jokes.punchline: Without glasses, Clark apparently resembles a girl — the worker says so directly and without filter
jokes.explanation: The joke lands on the worker's blunt honesty rather than anything particularly original. Clark's androgyny as a visual gag is functional. Angela's agreement makes it better.

jokes.text: Worker escalates: 'And you know what? I think you are developing. We should go and get you a training bra.'
jokes.setup: Worker has just called Clark a pretty girl
jokes.punchline: She escalates to suggesting he needs a training bra — treating the joke as a real developmental observation
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'training bra' is the right level of absurd — committed, specific, and delivered as genuine concern. Works better than the initial pretty-girl joke because of the escalation structure.

jokes.text: Angela and Clark are caught in their fake relationship ruse. The worker revokes the discount: 'Full price.' Angela protests — worker: 'Shush!' Angela's talking-head: 'Turns out I can't even be in a pretend relationship.'
jokes.setup: The worker figures out Angela and Clark aren't really a couple
jokes.punchline: Angela's confessional — 'Turns out I can't even be in a pretend relationship' — is a self-aware capsule of her entire character arc
jokes.explanation: The confessional line is brilliant for Angela specifically — given her complicated romantic history (secret affairs, failed engagements), the idea that she can't even fake a functional relationship is tragically funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: Oh, you guys both think this is funny? Well, you know what? No more discount. Full price.
jokes.setup: Angela and the nail tech are both laughing at Clark looking like a pretty girl
jokes.punchline: The nail tech sides with her co-conspirator and revokes the couples discount — Clark loses both his dignity and his discount
jokes.explanation: The twist that the nail tech revokes the discount while laughing is a satisfying escalation — Clark's humiliation has real-world consequences. The physical comedy of Clark being ganged up on by two women is implicit and funny.

jokes.text: Darryl and Kevin attempt to claim the couples discount. Worker: 'No discount for two men. Two men are not a couple.' Darryl: 'We are together, romantically.' Worker flatly refuses.
jokes.setup: Darryl and Kevin approach the counter to claim the couples discount
jokes.punchline: The worker's blunt refusal to accept two men as a couple creates a standoff; Darryl's over-earnest 'We are together, romantically' is the highlight
jokes.explanation: Darryl's formal phrasing ('romantically') is funny given his earlier protest. The situation is a classic cringe standoff. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Darryl's speech to the nail salon worker: 'Him and me, all right, we are crazy in love. More in love than your small mind can comprehend. And we have two disposable incomes and no kids, and we're taking our business elsewhere.'
jokes.setup: The nail salon worker refuses to honor the discount for two men
jokes.punchline: Darryl's impassioned defense escalates from romance to economics ('two disposable incomes and no kids') as his primary argument for gay acceptance — the pivot to finances is the joke
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'crazy in love' to 'small mind' to 'two disposable incomes and no kids' is well-constructed. The economic argument as the climax of a gay rights speech is the unexpected twist that makes it funny — Darryl is simultaneously defending the couple and making a consumer threat. Very Darryl.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam arrive at the restaurant. Brian: 'Sorry we're late.' Brian: 'Oh, uh, no problem. I finished all the bread.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam apologize for being late to the Valentine's lunch
jokes.punchline: Brian casually mentions he ate all the bread — a socially graceless but oddly endearing response that deflates the formality of the reunion
jokes.explanation: Small, well-placed character detail. Eating all the bread is a recognizable social embarrassment delivered without embarrassment. Sets a slightly awkward tone for the lunch.

jokes.text: Jim suggests Brian could 'boom his whole life' for Jim's deaf father-in-law, then asks 'Does he pay well?'
jokes.setup: Jim is apologizing for Brian losing his job and trying to find him work
jokes.punchline: Jim's absurd suggestion to 'boom' his deaf father-in-law's entire life, followed by Brian's instant 'does he pay well?' — both characters treat the absurd premise as a real job lead
jokes.explanation: Good economy. Jim's Jim-ness — turning a genuine apology into a half-jokey non-solution — is perfectly in character. Brian's practical response maintains the bit well.

jokes.text: Brian reveals Alyssa isn't coming, then: 'Actually, we're not gonna make it.' — then cut to Dwight presenting another sales order to imaginary Andy.
jokes.setup: Brian announces his wife won't make the lunch
jokes.punchline: The reveal that they're splitting up lands like a gut punch — immediately cut to Dwight's comic routine with pretend Andy, creating tonal whiplash
jokes.explanation: The cut from Brian's sad revelation to Dwight doing 'Rink-a-dink deet deet doo' is good editing comedy — the juxtaposition heightens both moments. The mockumentary form makes this kind of structural joke possible.

jokes.text: Why, thank you, Mr. Schrute. I don't know how you do it. — You're a God. — Rink-a-dink, deet, deet, doo.
jokes.setup: Dwight has returned to his pretend-Andy office game
jokes.punchline: He's now playing both roles again, complimenting himself and calling himself a God, still punctuated with the Andy humming
jokes.explanation: The running gag lands again with the escalation that Dwight has now told himself he's 'a God.' Slightly diminishing returns from the first iteration but still charming.

jokes.text: Andy walks in. Dwight says 'You're back.' Beat. 'And you're disgusting.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just been contentedly role-playing with imaginary Andy when real Andy appears
jokes.punchline: Dwight's greeting is a flat assessment — 'you're disgusting' — presumably reacting to Andy's post-boat-trip appearance, delivered without ceremony
jokes.explanation: Three words after a beat — maximum economy. The callback to Dwight's imaginary perfect Andy makes real Andy's disgusting arrival funnier. Dwight's ability to offer a greeting and an insult simultaneously is quintessentially him.

jokes.text: Unnamed worker: 'Oh geez, my nails aren't dry yet. I don't think I can work for at least a couple hours.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just returned and is about to reassert authority
jokes.punchline: Someone uses their nail appointment as cover to avoid working — transparently false excuse delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Minor background gag. Functional but not specific enough to any character to land big.

jokes.text: Andy's entrance: 'Well, well, well, look who it is. Andy. I guess I can cancel my order from zappos.com because, oh, the loafers have arrived.'
jokes.setup: Andy walks in on his own employees who weren't expecting him
jokes.punchline: Andy refers to himself in the third person and calls himself 'the loafers' — the preppy-guy self-burn is cheerfully oblivious
jokes.explanation: Andy calling himself 'the loafers' — both a shoe reference and a slacker slur — is nicely self-aware in a characteristically Andy-oblivious way. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Erin's talking-head: 'I am really, really bad at breakups. Technically, I'm still dating my first-grade boyfriend. I mean, we just had our 20th anniversary. And I forgot to get him something.'
jokes.setup: Erin has failed to break up with Andy and hugged him warmly instead
jokes.punchline: She reveals she's been 'dating' her first-grade boyfriend for 20 years because she never broke up with him — and feels guilty about forgetting their anniversary
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The idea that Erin has been technically dating her first-grade boyfriend for 20 years because she can't break up with people is perfectly absurd — but what elevates it is the guilt about forgetting their anniversary. It's not just a weird premise; it's a character portrait. Only Erin could deliver this. Rivals the dying-dog and chunky-lemon-milk jokes for episode peak.

jokes.text: Andy plays bembe drums and sings 'Yoruba yoruba / aruba yoruba' while wearing what sounds like island-influenced clothing, and tells Erin to 'clop the cloppers.'
jokes.setup: Andy has returned from Turks and Caicos with indigenous island instruments as a Valentine's gift
jokes.punchline: The instruments are bamboo percussion; Andy performs with full commitment while everyone watches uncomfortably; 'clop the cloppers' is an absurdly specific instruction
jokes.explanation: A strong cringe set piece. Andy's oblivious performative enthusiasm while the office watches in horror is classic Andy. 'Clop the cloppers' is a funny phrase. The discomfort is the joke and it's well-sustained.

jokes.text: Pete's line to Andy: 'Hey, burning man, if it's not selling out too much, you might wanna throw on a tie. David Wallace is gonna be here in an hour.'
jokes.setup: Andy is playing island music in what is presumably disheveled beach attire
jokes.punchline: 'Burning man' as a nickname for Andy's current state is exactly calibrated — it's an insult that also describes the look precisely
jokes.explanation: 'Burning man' is a good nickname that lands because of its specificity. The politeness of 'if it's not selling out too much' is a nice softener that makes Pete's understatement sharper.

jokes.text: Andy insists Wallace knows about the three-month absence. Nellie: 'Wallace does know that you've been gone for the last three months?' Andy: 'I have no idea. I don't know what he knows or doesn't know.' Then: 'It's not hard to get high-speed internet in Turks and Caicos, people. It's in every bembe cafe.'
jokes.setup: Andy claims he and Wallace have 'been in touch the whole time'
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately reverses — 'I have no idea what he knows' — then pivots to defending Turks and Caicos internet infrastructure to justify his indefensible behavior
jokes.explanation: Andy's instant self-contradiction — claiming total contact, then admitting total ignorance — is perfect characterization of his delusional self-protective thinking. 'Every bembe cafe' is a great absurd detail that shows Andy has absorbed his trip's culture while missing all practical responsibilities.

jokes.text: It's not hard to get high-speed internet in Turks and Caicos, people. It's in every bembe cafe.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to justify why being in the Caribbean for three months wasn't an excuse for lost communication
jokes.punchline: 'It's in every bembe cafe' — Andy casually references the island instrument cafe as if it's a common reference point for everyone
jokes.explanation: Andy's seamless integration of 'bembe cafe' as an assumed shared reference is perfectly oblivious. It also reveals that Andy has fully absorbed a new culture he's about to abandon. Character-specific and self-undermining.

jokes.text: Andy asks where Jim is. Told he's at Valentine's lunch. 'For two hours, really?' — Dwight: 'So, you're concerned about peoples' long absence from their place of work. If the shoe fits...'
jokes.setup: Andy questions Jim taking two hours for a Valentine's lunch
jokes.punchline: Dwight's devastating callback — 'if the shoe fits' — for a man who just returned from three months away questioning a two-hour lunch
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured. The setup is Andy's oblivious complaint, the punchline is Dwight wielding the irony with surgical precision. 'If the shoe fits' is economical and devastating. This joke writes itself but is executed perfectly — Andy walking right into this is exactly in character, and Dwight seizing the moment is exactly in character.

jokes.text: So, you're concerned about peoples' long absence from their place of work.
jokes.setup: Andy has questioned Jim's two-hour Valentine's lunch
jokes.punchline: Dwight calls out the obvious hypocrisy — Andy lecturing about long absences after a three-month boat trip
jokes.explanation: Dwight's ironic observation is perfectly timed and cuts Andy at exactly the right moment. The delivery as a calm, almost bureaucratic observation ('concerned about people's long absence') makes it cut harder than a direct attack would.

jokes.text: Andy plays bembe in the background while Jim makes his dry observation — the musical percussion punctuating the uncomfortable moment.
jokes.setup: Jim is making a pointed comment about Andy questioning his absence.
jokes.punchline: Andy is simultaneously playing 'Yoruba yoruba' on his clappers, oblivious, providing absurd musical accompaniment to his own humiliation.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Andy playing island music while being diplomatically skewered is strong layered comedy. The audience gets both Jim's wit and Andy's oblivious percussive accompaniment simultaneously. This kind of background visual comedy is a mockumentary specialty.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's awkward lunch with Brian — extended scene of them sitting with his relationship news. Jim's reaction beat: staring, processing, not knowing what to say.
jokes.setup: Brian has just revealed he and his wife are splitting up at a Valentine's Day lunch
jokes.punchline: The audience sees Jim and Pam sitting with this information — the Valentine's Day setting makes the announcement maximally uncomfortable; the silence IS the joke
jokes.explanation: The Valentine's Day context makes this beat land — sitting with news of a breakup at a couples' restaurant is inherently uncomfortable and funny. Mostly serves dramatic purposes but earns a mild laugh.

jokes.text: Brian: 'We have to find a different way to communicate other than breaking down in front of each other.' Then adds: 'At least my crying won't get you fired.'
jokes.setup: Brian notes that he and Jim keep meeting emotionally — but Brian got fired for his emotional intervention in the warehouse
jokes.punchline: 'At least my crying won't get you fired' is self-deprecating gallows humor about his own job loss
jokes.explanation: Good dark beat. Brian using humor to process his firing is natural, and the line has a nice self-aware sadness to it. Works better dramatically than comedically but qualifies as a joke.

jokes.text: Andy demands Dwight say 'coolio.' Dwight refuses. Andy escalates, saying it repeatedly. Dwight: 'Not a word.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks if they're 'coolio' after the confrontation
jokes.punchline: Dwight's refusal to validate 'coolio' as a word — even under repeated pressure — is a principled stand on linguistics in the middle of a professional conflict
jokes.explanation: Dwight's pedantry about 'coolio' not being a word is perfect Dwight. The escalation — Andy repeating it more desperately, Dwight remaining unmoved — is well-structured. The word itself is funny through repetition.

jokes.text: Andy calls Jan to 'clear up' the Scranton White Pages deal. He says 'coolio' to Jan mid-call while the deal collapses.
jokes.setup: Andy insists on calling Jan to resolve the pricing issue, against everyone's advice
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the increasingly catastrophic call, Andy says 'Coolio. I'm coolio.' to Jan — the absurd word choice deployed at the worst possible moment
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback structure. Dwight refuses to say 'coolio' on principle; Andy immediately uses 'coolio' on a business call with the company's biggest client as the deal falls apart. The joke layers comedy (the word's absurdity) with character failure (Andy's oblivious self-sabotage) and callback payoff. Strong episode moment.

jokes.text: Jan invokes her 30-day exit clause and cancels the contract. Andy pleads: 'Jan, please do not listen to this boob! Remember Clark. He gave you everything. Everything.' Clark, on the phone: 'Jan, I don't know what he's talking about, but--'
jokes.setup: The deal is collapsing; Andy tries to save it
jokes.punchline: Andy throws Clark under the bus with a vague but damning endorsement ('he gave you everything, everything') — Clark's horrified denial makes it worse
jokes.explanation: 'He gave you everything. Everything.' implies Clark did something highly inappropriate to make the sale, and Andy broadcasting this on a speakerphone call is a great cringe escalation. Clark's 'I don't know what he's talking about' is the right panicked response.

jokes.text: Andy: 'That was not... how I had hoped that would go.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just caused the branch's biggest sale to collapse in under two minutes
jokes.punchline: His only response is a masterpiece of understatement — delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom understatement. Works because of the contrast between the magnitude of the disaster and Andy's genteel assessment. Economy is almost perfect — any more words would ruin it.

jokes.text: Andy breezes back into the bullpen: 'Hey everybody. Great job. Listen, we're a smidge behind on my paychecks.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just destroyed the branch's biggest deal
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to demanding his 12 missed paychecks as if this is the pressing issue — the obliviousness is staggering
jokes.explanation: 'A smidge' is doing heavy lifting here. Andy framing 12 missed paychecks as 'a smidge behind' while having just tanked the biggest sale is perfect character obliviousness. 'Great job' before asking for money is also a nice tonal absurdity.

jokes.text: Oscar deadpans: 'Yes, well, as you know, we get paid on Fridays. And you haven't been here for 12 Fridays.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks about being behind on paychecks
jokes.punchline: Oscar walks him through the elementary math with accountant-level patience — the condescension is the joke
jokes.explanation: Oscar's accountant precision weaponized as condescension is very him. The patience of explaining 'you haven't been here for 12 Fridays' to a grown man is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Wallace gives Andy a bonus check. Kevin specifies: 'Quarter's three months. That's how long you've been gone.' Multiple people in the office say 'Mm-hmm' in unison.
jokes.setup: Andy receives a bonus check for the branch exceeding targets — the branch he abandoned for three months
jokes.punchline: Kevin's precise translation, followed by the group's synchronized passive-aggressive 'Mm-hmm' chorus, communicates maximum judgment without confrontation
jokes.explanation: The group 'Mm-hmm' is beautifully choreographed passive aggression. Kevin translating 'quarter' to 'three months' and then to 'how long you've been gone' is perfectly escalating specificity. The whole office communally savaging Andy through pure 'mm-hmm' is a lovely ensemble moment.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking-head: 'Two seconds of the turd dog, and he loses the biggest sale this branch has ever seen. Do you have any idea what I had to do to get that sale from Jan? I mean, I went all out. All out. I mean like everything was out the whole week.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is furious about losing the White Pages deal
jokes.punchline: 'Everything was out the whole week' strongly implies Dwight did something sexually inappropriate with Jan to make the sale — the ambiguity is deliberate and the horror is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Everything was out the whole week' is beautifully constructed implication. Dwight's wounded pride about his mysterious efforts — which we are clearly meant to interpret as sexual — is funnier for being half-stated. The callback to Clark's line ('he gave you everything') compounds the implication.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'He just waltzes back in here like he owns the chunky lemon milk.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is furious at Andy's return
jokes.punchline: 'Like he owns the chunky lemon milk' repurposes Kevin's earlier gross detail as an expression of entitlement — it's a perfect callback that also makes no literal sense as a metaphor
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best callback and arguably its best line. 'Like he owns the chunky lemon milk' works as an expression of outrage because the milk was Kevin's, not Andy's — so it's also literally accurate that Andy thinks he owns it. The phrase is quotable, specific, and absurd as a metaphor. It rewards attentive viewers and works on first watch too. Near-elite sitcom writing.

jokes.text: Dwight's 'boy who cried wolf' speech: 'I'd like to rat out Andy, but unfortunately I have a bit of a boy who cried wolf dynamic with David Wallace. Except instead of a boy I'm a man, and instead of a wolf I cried genetically-engineered monster wolf.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants to tell Wallace about Andy but can't because of his credibility issues
jokes.punchline: His correction of the metaphor — 'not wolf, genetically-engineered monster wolf' — implies that whatever Dwight reported to Wallace before was so extreme it destroyed his credibility entirely
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's finest jokes. The 'genetically-engineered monster wolf' correction is Dwight at his most Dwight — the specificity of his delusion is the joke. He doesn't just cry wolf, he cries about a scientifically enhanced predator. The structure is textbook — set up the familiar metaphor, then subvert it with escalating specificity. Could only be Dwight. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jim says he won't rat on Andy. Meredith: 'Meredith Palmer ain't never been called no narc. Floozy? Yes. Alkie? Check. Einstein sarcastically? You bet. But never no narc. Vomit mop? Sure. Floor meat? That's me. Flesh hoover? Hi.'
jokes.setup: Jim asks if anyone will rat on Andy
jokes.punchline: Meredith delivers an escalating list of nicknames she's been called — each one worse than the last — culminating in 'flesh hoover' as a self-introduction. She's fine with all of them except narc.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a candidate for one of the great Meredith moments in the series. The escalating list of self-applied nicknames — each more horrifying than the last — is impeccably written. The structure builds: 'Floozy, Alkie' are relatively mild, 'vomit mop, floor meat' are disgusting, 'flesh hoover' is genuinely shocking. The joke is that she OBJECTS to 'narc' — the one harmless label — while accepting all the others with pride. 'Flesh hoover? Hi.' as a self-introduction is the peak. Kevin cutting her off ('that's more than plenty') and asking 'Why does no one stop her?' adds a perfect button. Near-perfect comedy writing.

jokes.text: Andy re-enters the bullpen playing bembe: 'What's going on in here, dirty players? Let's get back to bustin' some paper rhymes. Come on.' He plays the drums again.
jokes.setup: Andy walks into a tense bullpen where people are discussing how to handle his return
jokes.punchline: 'Bustin' some paper rhymes' — Andy's attempt at office-hip-hop while playing bamboo drums — is so tone-deaf to the room's mood that the cluelessness itself is funny
jokes.explanation: 'Bustin' some paper rhymes' is a funny line — it's Andy's attempt at urban office-party energy that lands completely flat. The persistent bembe is a good running gag.

jokes.text: Cut to Andy saying 'It's Andy.' — apparently playing/singing a riff on the 'Who's that girl?' pop song about himself.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to re-establish himself in the office with music and enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: He's apparently singing his own name to a pop song melody — the narcissism is both transparent and pathetic
jokes.explanation: Simple but effective character beat. Andy singing his own name to reclaim the room is a good visual/audio gag even in transcript form.

jokes.text: I guess I just feel like a chump... who knows less about his marriage than the sound guy.
jokes.setup: Jim explains why he's upset about the Brian situation
jokes.punchline: 'Who knows less about his marriage than the sound guy' — the self-deprecating precision of 'the sound guy' as the comparison point is both funny and devastating
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'the sound guy' — not 'another man' or 'a stranger' — makes this line. It's also meta-aware in a show about documentary filmmaking. Jim's humiliation is precise and real, and the understatement of calling it 'being a chump' while the reality is much heavier gives it its dark comedy edge. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jim's sarcastic 'Yeah, well, yeah, okay. Well, then thank you. Thanks to both of you.' — directed at Pam and implicitly at Brian, after Pam explains she didn't share her crying because she didn't want to stress Jim out.
jokes.setup: Pam explains her reasoning; Jim realizes the explanation doesn't make him feel better.
jokes.punchline: 'Thanks to both of you.' — Jim extends the thanks to the sound guy who was present for what he wasn't — a sardonic, wounded inclusion of Brian.
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'Thanks to both of you' is a pointed passive-aggressive joke — he's thanking the sound guy who isn't there. The 'both of you' implies Brian as a third party in their marriage who received something Jim didn't. Darkly funny and character-rich.

jokes.text: Andy asks Nellie to brief him on highlights. Nellie mentions the Scranton White Pages. Andy: 'Not helpful. Let's stay positive, people.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks for highlights in case Wallace asks
jokes.punchline: The first thing mentioned is the deal Andy just destroyed — he immediately dismisses it as 'not helpful' and asks to 'stay positive' — pure Andy denial
jokes.explanation: Andy's ability to dismiss the consequence of his own actions with 'not helpful, stay positive' is a tight character joke. Quick and efficient.

jokes.text: Andy tells Wallace they were having a 'weekly round table where we motivate each other — I get as much out of it as they do.'
jokes.setup: Wallace walks in on Andy asking for gossip to prepare for their meeting
jokes.punchline: Andy instantly reframes the meeting preparation as a motivational round table — and claims to benefit from it too — the lie is improvised, transparent, and delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Andy's reflexive lying to authority figures is well-captured. 'I get as much out of it as they do' is the precise detail that makes the spin funnier — he's not just covering up, he's claiming personal growth.

jokes.text: We were just having our weekly round table where we motivate each other. I'm not gonna lie -- I get as much out of it as they do.
jokes.setup: Andy catches David Wallace with the office group and has to explain what they were doing (gossiping about Andy)
jokes.punchline: Andy spontaneously invents a 'weekly round table' that has never existed and immediately sells it hard, including self-congratulatory praise of his own leadership
jokes.explanation: Andy's ability to generate plausible-sounding corporate speak under pressure while including himself in a flattering light is very character-specific. 'I'm not gonna lie — I get as much out of it as they do' is the telling moment of self-insert.

jokes.text: Kevin tells Andy about Pam's mural fire: 'Lit the whole thing on fire. It was crazy.' Andy, confused: 'There was a fire in the warehouse? The whole thing is in ashes. Fire department was here. It was in all the papers.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks for highlights from his absence
jokes.punchline: Kevin casually mentions a warehouse fire as if it's a fun story; Andy's shock — 'it was in all the papers!' — highlights how completely disconnected he was from the office for three months
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — Kevin's casual 'it was crazy' vs Andy's genuine horror at learning of a major event he missed. The detail that it was in 'all the papers' underscores how truly absent Andy was.

jokes.text: Kevin reveals Kathy Ireland is now the 'official spokesbabe of Dunder Mifflin' — topless on European billboards. Wallace: 'Go, Kathy. She's like 50.' Kevin: 'They're tasteful.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is listing office highlights for Andy before the Wallace meeting — then Wallace himself walks in mid-briefing
jokes.punchline: Wallace endorsing topless Kathy Ireland billboards with 'Go, Kathy. She's like 50' — the executive enthusiasm is unexpected and slightly inappropriate — Kevin's 'They're tasteful' is the button
jokes.explanation: Wallace's enthusiasm for the topless billboards subverts his authority figure role. Kevin's 'they're tasteful' is the right defensive beat. The absurdity of 'spokesbabe' as an actual corporate title is the base joke.

jokes.text: And who knew the balloon game would be so lucrative? And thank God, right? We needed the income after the fire. — What fire? — The warehouse fire. Weren't you just down there? — It looked fine to me.
jokes.setup: Andy has casually mentioned 'the fire' in front of Wallace during the briefing
jokes.punchline: Wallace says it looked fine — Andy immediately realizes he's in a hole and starts trying to dig out
jokes.explanation: The speed at which Andy deploys his newly-acquired fire knowledge and immediately gets caught out is well-paced cringe comedy. 'It looked fine to me' sets up Andy's desperate metaphor spin.

jokes.text: Andy tells Wallace 'Think you'll agree I explained that pretty well' after his incoherent fire metaphor speech. Wallace: '[pause] Okay.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just delivered an incomprehensible explanation
jokes.punchline: Wallace's 'Okay' — presumably with a look — is a masterpiece of polite non-agreement. Andy takes it as validation.
jokes.explanation: One word. Maximum economy. Wallace's 'Okay' does everything — it's not agreement, it's barely acknowledgment, and the mockumentary format lets us imagine the accompanying look. Andy's self-assessment preceding it makes the 'Okay' devastating.

jokes.text: Andy and Erin's breakup scene: Andy insists on the relationship using fishing metaphors. 'Really playing the scales, huh?' Erin: 'I don't know, it just sort of sounds like noise to me now.' Andy: 'You think I need a new fish?'
jokes.setup: Andy plays their fish song for Erin as part of a romantic gesture
jokes.punchline: Erin's 'it sounds like noise' is meant about the relationship but Andy hears it as music criticism — he pivots to wondering if he needs a new fish
jokes.explanation: Nice double-meaning structure — Erin is talking about the relationship, Andy hears music criticism. 'You think I need a new fish?' is a good absurd literal response. The joke works because Andy's obliviousness is genuinely funny rather than just sad.

jokes.text: Erin: 'I don't love you anymore.' Andy: '[pause] What?' Erin: 'I still like you.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks what's wrong with the fish/relationship
jokes.punchline: Erin drops 'I don't love you anymore' completely flatly, then immediately softens with 'I still like you' — the rapid tonal shift is the joke
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Erin's delivery — she clearly thinks 'I still like you' is a meaningful consolation prize. Andy's 'What?' lands as both comedic reaction and genuine confusion. Very Erin — her emotional bluntness delivered with kindness is her signature.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You re-tweeted me a lot, to be fair.'
jokes.setup: Erin says Andy didn't email much during his trip
jokes.punchline: Andy cites re-tweets as evidence of romantic connection — retweets as a love language
jokes.explanation: Six words doing exceptional work. 'You re-tweeted me a lot, to be fair' as a defense of neglecting your girlfriend is both perfectly Andy and a precise satirical observation about social media as a substitute for actual intimacy. The 'to be fair' clinches it — he genuinely believes this counts.

jokes.text: Andy's breakup logic: 'My parents lasted 30, 40 years. They were never happy at the same time.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to convince Erin their out-of-sync feelings aren't a dealbreaker
jokes.punchline: Andy cites his parents' 30-40 year marriage as a model — immediately noting they were never happy simultaneously, which he presents as aspirational
jokes.explanation: 'They were never happy at the same time' as a model for a lasting relationship is a darkly brilliant observation delivered with complete Andy sincerity. It's accidentally insightful — marriages do often work this way — which makes it funnier. Good character integration; Andy's family dysfunction informing his relationship logic is consistent with his backstory.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I mean, what do we have left? 35, maybe 40 years, if we're lucky? I mean, I have spent a lot of time in the sun. You got really sunburned.' Erin: 'I'm gonna be a prune in like three years.'
jokes.setup: Andy is making an optimistic case for their long-term future
jokes.punchline: The long-term romantic pitch is immediately undercut by both of them acknowledging Andy's premature aging from sun damage — the prune timeline is three years
jokes.explanation: 'Prune in like three years' is a good specific beat. Both characters agreeing on the sun damage timeline while ostensibly discussing their romantic future is a nice non-sequitur that still feels organic.

jokes.text: What do we have left? 35, maybe 40 years, if we're lucky? I mean, I have spent a lot of time in the sun. You got really sunburned. — I'm gonna be a prune in like three years.
jokes.setup: Andy is arguing for the longevity of their relationship
jokes.punchline: Erin cheerfully agrees — 'I'm gonna be a prune in like three years' — reducing Andy's romantic argument to sun damage speculation
jokes.explanation: Erin's agreement that Andy will look like a prune in three years, delivered matter-of-factly during a breakup conversation, is an odd and funny beat. The specificity of 'three years' is good. Both characters have abandoned the emotional stakes to discuss dermatology.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I know you may not be feeling love for me right now, but if you fake it, I won't be able to tell the difference. So I'll feel good.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to salvage the relationship despite Erin's honesty
jokes.punchline: Andy's solution is for Erin to fake love — and he frames his inability to detect the deception as a feature, not a bug — 'I won't be able to tell the difference, so I'll feel good'
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent character comedy. Andy's pitch — 'fake it, I won't know, so I'll be happy' — is both a great joke and a devastating character portrait. He's describing a relationship built on willful ignorance as a positive solution. The line walks the line between funny and sad, which is The Office's sweet spot. High character integration and originality.

jokes.text: Jim suggests canceling the wine night: 'I just feel like I got a bunch of stuff to do in Philly, and I'm sure you have stuff to do, so we can just...' Pam: 'Drop me at the bus station?'
jokes.setup: Jim is clearly pulling back from the Valentine's Day evening
jokes.punchline: Pam completes his thought with 'drop me at the bus station?' — a response so deflatingly functional it exposes the state of their marriage
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Pam's completion of the sentence. Jim's vague 'I'm sure you have stuff to do' on Valentine's Day is already a red flag; Pam cutting straight to 'bus station' is funny and quietly heartbreaking. The economy is excellent — the bus station suggestion says everything about where they are.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I just feel like we're gonna fight.' Pam: 'Yeah.' Jim: 'So, how 'bout let's not?' Pam: 'Okay.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are clearly in tension but neither wants to confront it
jokes.punchline: Their agreement NOT to fight — delivered in flat, tired tones — IS the fight; the civility is the dysfunction
jokes.explanation: Good tonal comedy. The agreed-upon suppression of conflict is more awkward than the fight would be. Works better dramatically but earns a rueful laugh.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I don't think you should go to Philly tonight. I think you should stay, and I think we should fight.' Pam: 'You really want to fight on Valentine's Day?' Jim: 'Yeah, I do.' Beat. 'Okay. All right, put your dukes up, Beesly.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been avoiding conflict all episode; now he declares they should fight
jokes.punchline: 'Put your dukes up, Beesly' — Jim turns a sincere emotional moment into a playful boxing challenge, his classic deflection-via-charm, but this time it's in service of honesty
jokes.explanation: 'Put your dukes up, Beesly' is Jim at his most Jim — the joke is how he processes even serious emotional moments through playfulness. Using Pam's maiden name 'Beesly' is the specific touch that makes it feel like a callback to early-series Jim/Pam dynamics. Emotionally resonant AND funny. Strong moment.

jokes.text: Erin comes to Pete after failing to break up with Andy. Pete: 'Oh.' Erin: 'I'm sorry.' Pete: 'Oh, you don't have to apologize. I just — I just want you to be happy, okay?'
jokes.setup: Erin has spent the whole episode building up to breaking up with Andy and goes to Pete after
jokes.punchline: The failed breakup lands in Pete's 'Oh.' — one syllable carrying disappointment, acceptance, and compassion simultaneously — the silence and the 'oh' together are the joke
jokes.explanation: Pete's 'Oh' is beautifully understated, but this is primarily a dramatic beat with a comedic undercurrent. The comedy is in the awkwardness of the situation rather than a joke per se.

jokes.text: We're breaking up. And just so you know, I was worried that you were dead. You were gone for three months.
jokes.setup: Erin finally manages to break up with Andy
jokes.punchline: She adds 'I was worried you were dead' — the most alarming thing she's apparently been keeping to herself, delivered as a footnote to the breakup
jokes.explanation: The 'And just so you know, I was worried that you were dead' is a magnificent afterthought. The structure — breakup first, existential concern second — is perfectly Erin. The matter-of-fact 'You were gone for three months' as elaboration is the button. It reveals how much she's been holding in while also being very funny in its sequencing. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Erin's confession to Andy: 'We're breaking up. And just so you know, I was worried that you were dead. You were gone for three months.'
jokes.setup: Erin finally manages to break up with Andy
jokes.punchline: Her addendum — 'just so you know, I was worried you were dead' — is the unexpected coda; she's breaking up with him AND filing a welfare complaint simultaneously
jokes.explanation: 'Just so you know, I was worried you were dead' as a post-breakup addendum is very Erin — the concern for his wellbeing coexists with the dumping. It's a character-specific non-sequitur that reveals her fundamental warmth even in rejection. Good economy.

jokes.text: Wallace appears from around the corner: 'Andy? David. Still here. What was that about three months?'
jokes.setup: Erin breaks up with Andy and mentions he was gone three months — presumably believing they're alone
jokes.punchline: Wallace has been standing there the whole time — his casual 'still here' followed by the loaded question about three months is a perfect cold-close gut punch
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural punchline. 'Still here' is two words that do everything — it reveals Wallace's presence, implies he heard the whole thing, and sets up the devastating final question. 'What was that about three months?' closes the loop on the episode's central irony (Andy's absence being rewarded while he almost got away with it). The structure is nearly perfect as a cold-close joke. Economy is exceptional. Rewatch bonus because you can see it coming only in retrospect.

tmdb_overview: The staffers pair up as faux couples to score a Valentine's Day discount at a mall. Erin tells Pete that she'll break up with Andy when he returns, but Pete has his doubts. Jim and Pam socialize with the documentary's soundman.
